item.title: Organizing Sustainably with Nature in the Global South
item.content:encoded:
Simone Barakat, Fundação Getulio Vargas

Maria Ehrnström-Fuentes, Hanken School of Economics

Seray Ergene, University of Rhode Island

Steffen Farny, Leuphana University Luneburg

Judy Muthuri, University of the West Indies

Contemporary sustainability challenges increasingly foreground organizations as embedded within complex social-ecological systems rather than operating independently from them. While ecological degradation and resource constraints affect organizations worldwide, these challenges are more immediate and structurally embedded in the operating environments of the Global South. These challenges are not just a background context to which organizations must adapt but an outcome of long-standing patterns of extraction, uneven development, and entrenched social inequalities that continue to shape what sustainability can mean in practice.

Although sustainability has gained prominence in Management and Organization Studies in recent years, the field continues to draw predominantly on Global North epistemologies, experiences, and assumptions. While important exceptions engage with ecocentric, posthumanist, and indigenous approaches to organizing, sustainability research in MOS remains overwhelmingly theorized from Global North contexts, leaving many southern voices and experiences marginalized. This marginalization does not imply an absence of sustainability-oriented organizing in the Global South. On the contrary, a growing body of work examines organizing in the Global South in ways that directly address issues such as environmental degradation, community resilience, and socio-ecological justice. However, much of this work is not explicitly framed as "sustainability" research and therefore remains peripheral to mainstream MOS debates. Consequently, despite rich empirical insights, we still lack a robust understanding of how organizations in the Global South pursue sustainability under conditions of severe climate vulnerabilities and entrenched power asymmetries.

Recent developments in sustainability scholarship have brought to the fore regenerative forms of organizing that recognize the interdependence among economic activity and ecological integrity. This scholarship emphasizes place-based practices that work with nature and that cultivate resilience and long-term ecological viability. Such forms of organizing have long existed in the Global South, grounded in relational understandings of land, community, and more-than-human worlds. This marginalization of southern voices raises ethical questions about who gets to define what is considered 'sustainable' and how the dominance of northern perspectives not only marginalizes stakeholders and their visions but also determines who benefits from how this concept is defined.

Engaging with sustainability practices and knowledges from the Global South provides an urgently needed ground for expanding and challenging the conceptual foundations of how sustainability is theorized and made sense of in organizational contexts that are marked by contradictions and vulnerabilities that are often not visible in (but also part of) the Global North. A better understanding of southern perspectives on sustainability can fundamentally expand existing theories and thus shape MOS research and debates beyond the Global South.

This Special Issue responds to the dearth in the literature by inviting both theoretical and empirical submissions on how sustainability is organized and defined in the Global South. The Special Issue broadly understands Global South as both an empirical location which is "apart and distinct from North America and Europe [and Australia]" and as a "challenge to universalist knowledge" where scholars reformulate concepts around sustainability based on empirical accounts and voices from the Global South. The Global North and Global South are not separated by a strict boundary; rather, these organizational contexts are marked by friction and interdependence. This allows research to focus on and articulate sustainability definitions and organizing processes that are upheld by North-South relations, such as global supply chains or environmental governance.

The Special Issue is particularly interested in work that considers the embeddedness of organizations within social–ecological systems and that engages sustainability not as a generic concern, but as a core organizing challenge shaped by place and history. The Special Issue aims to advance a pluralistic perspective from multiple contexts, theories, and concepts instead of a unifying theory for all communities on all continents. Submissions may draw on diverse theoretical traditions and methodological approaches, including those grounded in indigenous, decolonial, relational, posthumanist, or other traditional ecological knowledge pertinent to the Global South, and may focus on organizations of various forms, including firms, cooperatives, social enterprises, community organizations, and hybrid arrangements.

In sum, this Special Issue aims to generate organizational knowledge that is both theoretically generative and practically relevant for organizing sustainability in a world of multiple crises.

Potential topics

  • Organizing for Environmental Sustainability across Communities and Regions - How do communities and organizations work together to govern natural resources and shared ecological commons?
  • How do sustainability standards, certifications, and supply-chain rules influence organizational practices across regions?
  • How do organizations manage environmental interdependencies across local and global contexts?
  • What challenges arise when local ecological priorities clash with global market or regulatory pressures, and how do organizations deal with these challenges in practice?
  • Organizing with Nature from a Global South perspective - How do organizations in the Global South manage their activities within the carrying ecological capacity of the planet (i.e., planetary boundaries), particularly under conditions of resource constraints and institutional fragility?
  • How do organizations in the Global South engage with degrowth, sufficiency, circular, or regenerative practices?
  • What tensions do organizations in the Global South face between economic survival and ecological realities, and how do they navigate these circumstances in practice?
  • How organizations in the Global South conceptualize and manage their embeddedness within social–ecological systems and attempt to develop a regenerative dynamic with nature?
  • Power, Inequality, and the Governance of Nature - What are the sources of environmental injustices currently in the global South? How are they experienced? What are some resistances to these injustices, and how do they unfold? What are some policy mechanisms (if any) to address these injustices?
  • How do power asymmetries manifest in sustainability governance and transnational regulations?
  • How do corporations influence environmental policy and access to natural resources?
  • How do resistance and counter-organizing emerge around contested environmental futures?
  • Stakeholders and Environmental Sustainability from a Global South Perspective - How do organizations in the Global South engage with stakeholders in relation to environmental sustainability?
  • How are the interests of diverse stakeholders, such as communities, governments, NGOs, and other stakeholders, navigated around environmental risks and resource use?
  • How do stakeholder relationships influence organizational decisions and practices related to environmental sustainability?
  • How do power asymmetries and dependency relations among stakeholders shape environmental outcomes and organizing processes?

Timeline

  • October 20, 2026: Paper Development Workshop
  • February 28, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline

item.title: New Vistas for Human Resources Management Research in the Global South
item.content:encoded:
Edwina Pio, Auckland University of Technology

Stephen Kalilpakdee, Assumption University of Thailand

This special issue seeks to advance Human Resources Management (HRM) research by centering perspectives, experiences, and contexts from the Global South. While HRM scholarship has traditionally been dominated by Western theoretical frameworks and assumptions, there is a critical need to develop contextually-grounded HRM knowledge that reflects the unique institutional, economic, social, and cultural realities of countries and regions in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East, and other parts of the Global South.

The special issue welcomes empirical studies, theoretical contributions, critical reviews, and methodological innovations that challenge dominant HRM paradigms and offer new insights into how organizations manage human resources in Global South contexts. We are particularly interested in research that moves beyond adapting Western HRM models and instead develops indigenous, culturally-sensitive, and locally-relevant approaches to understanding people management.

Contributors are encouraged to engage with diverse epistemologies, research methodologies, and analytical frameworks that honor the complexity and diversity of HRM practices across the Global South. This includes qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, and participatory action research approaches that center local voices and experiences.

Potential topics

  • Exploring alternative theoretical frameworks and paradigms for HRM in the Global South
  • Indigenous and culturally-rooted HRM approaches and practices
  • HRM in informal economies and non-traditional work arrangements
  • Human agency, worker voice, and resistance in HRM systems
  • HRM's role in addressing inequality, social justice, and sustainable development
  • Technology, digitalization, and their impacts on HRM in emerging economies
  • HRM in post-colonial and transitional contexts
  • Labor standards, worker protection, and ethical HRM practices in the Global South
  • Comparative HRM studies across Global South regions
  • Organizational learning and knowledge management in Global South contexts

Timeline

  • December 1, 2026: Submission window
